# From separate interpolations to a common isoparametric implementation {#sec-common-isoparametric-axial-bar}

::: {.callout-note}
## Repository snapshot

**Course edition:** 2026--27\
**Starting snapshot:** `2026-27/S08-three-node-quadratic-bar`\
**Target snapshot:** `2026-27/S09-common-isoparametric-axial-bar`
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Task"}
Compare the verified linear and quadratic isoparametric axial-bar
implementations. Keep the interpolation choice explicit, but replace only the
operations that have become demonstrably common with one shared implementation.
:::

In S07 and S08, the linear and quadratic numerical formulations were
deliberately kept separate so that the effect of changing the interpolation
remained visible in the implementation. With both formulations now understood
and verified, we can compare them and ask:

> Which differences belong to the interpolation, and which operations are the
> same finite element algorithm acting on different data?

No new finite element operations are introduced here. Instead, we will reuse the
procedures developed in the preceding chapters and identify which parts of the
implementation can now be shared.

## Start from the verified implementations

Run the regression suite before changing the source:

```text
julia test/runtests.jl
```

Resolve any baseline failure before continuing. The mathematical models and
reference results are already verified; S09 changes the organization of the
numerical implementation.

The separate numerical formulation files used in S07 and S08 were:

```text
examples/axial_bar_gauss_legendre_fem.jl
examples/quadratic_axial_bar_gauss_legendre_fem.jl
```

In S09, these are replaced by the common implementation

```text
src/isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
```

which serves both the linear and quadratic isoparametric formulations. The two
executable examples remain separate:

```text
examples/linear_isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
examples/quadratic_isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
```

The earlier implementations remain recoverable from the snapshots

```text
2026-27/S07-gauss-legendre-quadrature
2026-27/S08-three-node-quadratic-bar
```

Inspect the two snapshot implementations side by side. For each operation below,
decide whether changing from linear to quadratic interpolation requires a
different algorithm, or only different interpolation data or array dimensions.

  | Operation                             | What changes? |
  | ------------------------------------- | ------------- |
  | Shape functions and $d\mathbf N/d\xi$ |               |
  | Number of element DOFs                |               |
  | $J = (d\mathbf N/d\xi)\mathbf x_e$    |               |
  | $\mathbf B = (1/J)d\mathbf N/d\xi$    |               |
  | Gauss--Legendre integration           |               |
  | Local-to-global assembly              |               |
  | Global solution and reaction recovery |               |
  | Response recovery                     |               |

Do not assume that different array sizes or numerical values necessarily imply
different algorithms. Use the comparison to identify which parts of the two
implementations should remain interpolation-specific and which can be shared.

## Make interpolation the explicit variation

The first difference to isolate is the interpolation itself. Rather than
maintaining separate element procedures, we make the interpolation choice an
explicit input:

```julia
bar_shape_functions(xi, interpolation)
```

Here, `xi` is the reference coordinate and `interpolation` is either `"linear"`
or `"quadratic"`. The function returns the shape functions and their derivatives
with respect to the reference coordinate:

```text
N
dN_dxi
```

For linear interpolation,

$$
  \mathbf N(\xi) = \begin{bmatrix}
                     (1 - \xi)/2 \\
                     (1 + \xi)/2
                   \end{bmatrix},
  \qquad \frac{d\mathbf N}{d\xi} = \begin{bmatrix}
                                     -1/2 \\
                                     +1/2
                                   \end{bmatrix}.
$$

For quadratic interpolation, with the local nodes ordered as left endpoint,
midpoint, and right endpoint,

$$
  \mathbf N(\xi) = \begin{bmatrix}
                     \tfrac12\xi(\xi - 1) \\
                     1 - \xi^2 \\
                     \tfrac12\xi(\xi + 1)
                   \end{bmatrix},
  \qquad \frac{d\mathbf N}{d\xi} = \begin{bmatrix}
                                     \xi - \tfrac12 \\
                                     -2\xi \\
                                     \xi + \tfrac12
                                   \end{bmatrix}.
$$

These expressions were derived in the preceding chapters and do not need to be
reconsidered here. They are simply the interpolation-specific information
supplied to the common element procedure.

Once $\mathbf N$ and $d\mathbf N/d\xi$ are available, we can ask whether any of
the remaining isoparametric operations actually need to know whether the
interpolation is linear or quadratic.

## Build the common element procedure

The common element procedure is implemented by

```julia
integrate_axial_bar_gauss_legendre(
    x_e,
    E_e,
    A_e,
    q_e,
    num_gauss_legendre_points,
    interpolation,
)
```

which returns `K_e, f_e`.

The important change is that the size of the element arrays is no longer
hard-coded separately for each interpolation:

```julia
num_element_dofs = length(x_e)

K_e = zeros(num_element_dofs, num_element_dofs)
f_e = zeros(num_element_dofs)
```

For the present axial-bar elements, with one displacement DOF per node,
`num_element_dofs` is therefore 2 for a linear element and 3 for a quadratic
element. It is an element-level quantity and should not be confused with the
already established `total_dofs`, which refers to the complete assembled model.

The same implementation can therefore operate on either a two-node or a
three-node element without separate local-array definitions or loop limits.

### Represent the distributed load at the element nodes

The common element procedure receives `q_e` as the distributed-load values at
the element nodes and interpolates them using the selected shape functions.

For the present benchmarks, `element_q[e]` stores the constant distributed load
assigned to element `e`. The corresponding nodal values are constructed as

```julia
q_e = fill(element_q[e], num_element_dofs)
```

so that a uniform load $q$ gives

```text
linear:     q_e = [q, q]
quadratic:  q_e = [q, q, q]
```

More generally, `q_e` may contain different nodal values. The previously
verified linearly varying load for the two-node element is therefore handled by
the same element procedure, without an interpolation-specific branch.

Using the displacement shape functions to interpolate the prescribed load is
convenient for the present examples, but it is not a general requirement that
all physical fields use the same interpolation.

## Reuse the surrounding FEM workflow

Once the element procedure has been made independent of the interpolation order,
the surrounding finite element workflow can also be shared.

The common assembly procedure is implemented by

```julia
assemble_axial_bar_gauss_legendre!(
    K,
    f,
    node_coordinates,
    element_connectivity,
    element_E,
    element_A,
    element_q,
    num_gauss_legendre_points,
    interpolation,
)
```

It constructs the element quantities and uses the established assembly
operations

```julia
assemble_matrix!(K, K_e, dof_map)
assemble_vector!(f, f_e, dof_map)
```

for both linear and quadratic elements. The number of entries in `dof_map`
changes with the element interpolation, but the assembly procedure does not.

Similarly,

```julia
solve_axial_bar_gauss_legendre(
    node_coordinates,
    element_connectivity,
    element_E,
    element_A,
    element_q,
    applied_forces,
    constrained_dofs,
    prescribed_displacements,
    num_gauss_legendre_points,
    interpolation,
)
```

returns `u, reactions` using the same established global solution procedure for
both interpolation choices.

Response recovery is handled by

```julia
recover_axial_bar_response(
    node_coordinates,
    element_connectivity,
    element_E,
    element_A,
    u,
    response_reference_coordinates,
    interpolation,
)
```

which returns `response_coordinates, strain, stress, axial_force`.

The response coordinates are specified independently of the Gauss--Legendre
quadrature rule. Quadrature points are chosen to integrate the element
contributions, whereas response points are chosen to inspect the computed
solution. They may coincide, but one choice does not determine the other.

## Resulting source organization

The distinction between reusable finite element operations and executable
examples is now reflected in the repository structure:

```text
src/
    MiniFEM.jl
    two_springs_fem.jl
    axial_bar_closed_form.jl
    fem_assembly.jl
    gauss_legendre_quadrature.jl
    isoparametric_axial_bar.jl

examples/
    two_springs.jl
    four_element_axial_bar.jl
    gauss_legendre_scalar_integration.jl
    linear_isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
    quadratic_isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
```

The files in `src/` contain reusable FEM and numerical operations, whereas the
files in `examples/` define and run particular problems.

For the axial bar, the closed-form implementation

```text
src/axial_bar_closed_form.jl
```

is used by

```text
examples/four_element_axial_bar.jl
```

while the common isoparametric implementation

```text
src/isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
```

is used by both

```text
examples/linear_isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
examples/quadratic_isoparametric_axial_bar.jl
```

The examples still include the required source files explicitly with
`include(...)`. `src/MiniFEM.jl` remains inactive at this stage.

## Verify the refactoring

The tests must follow the new source organization as well. The regression suite
now loads the reusable FEM and numerical operations from `src/`, including the
common isoparametric axial-bar implementation, while retaining the separate
verification cases developed in the preceding snapshots.

Run the regression suite:

```text
julia test/runtests.jl
```

All previously verified linear and quadratic results should remain unchanged.

## Reflection

Comparing the S07 and S08 implementations has allowed us to separate
interpolation-specific information from the finite element operations that can
be shared.

The common implementation now supports both linear and quadratic elements within
the same program structure, preparing the way for the study of approximation
error and convergence.
